title: How Jim Henson Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck profile filmmaker and puppeteer Jim Henson, framed as a companion to their earlier Muppets episode. They cover his Mississippi birth and Maryland college years (a home economics degree that offered puppet courses), early TV work and experimental short films including Time Piece and The Cube, his puppet commercial company in New York, Sesame Street, the innovations of platforming and foam puppets, The Muppet Show, Fraggle Rock, Muppet Babies, the Muppet Movie, The Dark Crystal, Labyrinth, The Jim Henson Hour and Storyteller, his death from a staph infection, and the later sale and ownership history of the Muppets and Sesame Street characters. The episode closes with a listener mail about the Dark Ages and the Islamic world.

segments.title: Opening banter and Henson's reputation
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with off-topic banter about sensitivity training videos, then discuss Jim Henson's reputation as a genuinely good person and a filmmaker first. They note this episode complements their earlier Muppets episode.

segments.title: Early life, college, and first TV work
segments.summary: Henson was born in 1936 in Mississippi and was inspired by his maternal grandmother's creative work. He was a fan of ventriloquism and TV, studied studio art, and graduated with a home economics degree since it was the only degree offering puppet making courses. He had local TV guest spots in high school, and The Muppets' predecessor show Sam and Friends debuted in 1955.

segments.title: Experimental films and The Cube
segments.summary: Henson made experimental short films, including Time Piece, which earned an Academy Award nomination. They also describe The Cube, a one-hour NBC Experiment in Television installment about a man trapped in a white room.

segments.title: Europe trip, commercials, and early Muppets
segments.summary: After college Henson toured Europe, where puppetry was treated more seriously, and he decided to pursue puppetry. He married Jane, they separated without divorcing, and he founded a commercial production company in New York in 1963, hiring Frank Oz and Jerry Juhl. He kept rights to his creations, so Cookie Monster, first made for a chip ad, stayed with him. Rolf the Dog started on Purina commercials and appeared on The Jimmy Dean Show.

segments.title: Sesame Street and television puppetry
segments.summary: In 1969 Henson was invited onto the Sesame Street pilot by Children's Television Workshop. He did not create the show but created many iconic characters and directed live-action shorts. Hosts discuss how TV let puppets move beyond the limits of live stages, and how platforming let performers stand up.

segments.title: Foam puppets, Center for Puppetry Arts, and Saturday Night Live
segments.summary: Henson's use of softer foam allowed expressive faces suited to close-ups on TV. The hosts mention the Center for Puppetry Arts in Atlanta, which received about five hundred puppets from Henson. Henson also had a brief stint on Saturday Night Live in season one.

segments.title: The Muppet Show, Fraggle Rock, and Muppet Babies
segments.summary: Henson's big break came with The Muppet Show, made in London with Lew Grade's ATV studios, and it was a hit with adults and children. Fraggle Rock, one of HBO's early original series, won Cable Ace and International Emmy awards. Muppet Babies was a cartoon the hosts discuss. Rubber Ducky reached number sixteen on the Billboard charts in 1970.

segments.title: Movies: Muppet Movie, Dark Crystal, Labyrinth
segments.summary: The hosts discuss The Muppet Movie, The Dark Crystal (co-directed by Frank Oz, based on Brian Froud's drawings, a box office disappointment later seen as a cult film), and Labyrinth, written by Terry Jones and rewritten by others including George Lucas, with David Bowie.

segments.title: Jim Henson Hour, Storyteller, and Kermit as a real character
segments.summary: Henson's late eighties shows The Jim Henson Hour and The Storyteller are discussed, including Dog City, a film noir puppet story narrated by Rolf. The hosts describe how Henson wanted puppets to feel alive, with Kermit appearing as a guest on talk shows and Henson pioneering the Henson Performance Control System.

segments.title: Death, legacy, and Muppets ownership history
segments.summary: Henson died of a staph infection that led to organ failure. Jane Henson founded the Jim Henson Legacy, and the family runs the foundation. Henson had planned to sell the company to Disney for 150 million dollars. His children sold the company, including Sesame Street characters, to a German media company in 2000, which bought it back in 2003. Disney later acquired the Muppets, and the Creature Shop still builds Sesame Street puppets.

segments.title: Listener mail: the Dark Ages and Islamic world
segments.summary: A listener named Matt writes that the Dark Ages were not dark outside Europe, citing Islamic scholarship, Arabic translations of Greek philosophy, algebra, and trigonometry. The hosts respond briefly and invite Middle Eastern topic suggestions.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck invite listeners to send topic suggestions and visit the show website.
